Title: High Court rejects bid for closed-door trial in civil suit over Bandar Utama school murder
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — The High Court today rejected a bid by the teenager acquitted of murdering his schoolmate Yap Shing Xuen at a Bandar Utama secondary school last year to have the entire civil suit heard in-camera, or in closed-door proceedings.
Judicial Commissioner Datuk Anand Ponnudurai said there was no basis for the broader order sought by the teenager, through his counsel, to hold the entire proceedings in-camera, excluding members of the media and anyone not directly involved in the case.
Anand said the court could not determine at this stage which witnesses would testify or the nature of their evidence, adding that the defendants could later apply for specific witnesses to testify in-camera if their evidence was likely to identify the teenager.
“The court is cognisant of the Child Act 2001, which restricts the reporting of details identifying a child, and also of the interest of justice and the public interest.
“There are many cases in which orders are granted to protect a child, but the proceedings are still conducted with the media allowed to report, subject to restrictions.
“Considering the nature of this case and the necessity to protect the child/first defendant (D1), I am of the view that a balancing act is required.
“While the child must be protected, I see no reason for a total ban on reporting. There will be benefits to the public in knowing what transpires and in the judgment,” he said in his ruling earlier today.
Nevertheless, Anand ordered a ban on publishing any information that could identify the teenager, and directed that all cause papers be sealed and kept confidential, accessible only to the parties and their solicitors.
He also ordered that the names of D1, his litigation representative and his parents be anonymised and referred to only by their initials.
Lawyer Surendra Ananth appeared for Yap’s family, while Nicholas Poon represented the teenager, Abraham Au appeared for the boy’s parents and senior federal counsel Liew Horng Bin represented the government agencies.
In the current lawsuit filed on October 1, Yap’s family — her mother (pic) and sister — claimed that breaches of duty of care contributed to her death in October last year. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Background
In the current lawsuit filed on October 1, Yap’s family — her mother and sister — claimed that breaches of duty of care contributed to her death in October last year.
Among those named are the boy himself, his parents, and several school authorities, including his homeroom teacher, the school principal, and teachers responsible for counselling and student affairs.
The family also named officers from the Petaling Utama district education office, the Selangor education department director, the director-general of education, the education minister, the registrar general of educational institutions and teachers, the director-general of health, the health minister, the women, family and community development minister and the government of Malaysia.
Yap’s mother, who is also suing as the estate administrator and in her own right, is seeking special damages totalling RM120,602 for her daughter’s funeral expenses from the named defendants jointly and separately.
She is also separately seeking general damages to be assessed by the High Court, including any other relief the court deems fit or appropriate.
On September 14, the Shah Alam High Court acquitted and discharged the teenager after finding he was of unsound mind at the time of the offence, and ordered him to be placed at Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta for a period subject to the Sultan of Selangor’s approval.
The Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) has since filed an appeal challenging the acquittal.

Title: DAP lawmaker condemns police action against lawyers over sharing of Noorizwan’s custodial death photos
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Jelutong MP RSN Rayer today criticised the police for opening an investigation against lawyers representing Noorizwan Zulkefly, the 42-year-old who died while in police custody.
Rayer suggested the investigation was a form of intimidation, as he defended their right to share the photos of Noorizwan’s body that his family’s lawyers alleged showed signs of blunt force trauma, including broken ribs and severe head and spinal injuries.
“There were reports that the lawyers who shared the photos of (Noorizwan’s) post-mortem are being investigated.
“This is an infringement and a violation of a counsel’s right to handle any case without fear or favour,” he said at a press conference in Parliament building here.
“I take seriously the police’s statement that the lawyers who shared those photos are being subject to investigation.
“As a lawyer myself, I’d like to state that we are legally empowered to protect the rights of anyone who comes to us for help.”
He urged Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution and the Attorney General to “intervene” as it is an incident that happened “under the Madani government”.
A pathologist’s preliminary findings indicated Noorizwan suffered severe injuries caused by blunt force trauma.
The injuries, according to the family’s lawyers, included six to seven broken ribs, spinal and severe head injuries, bleeding in the brain and intestines, as well as bruising and swelling.
The case prompted Bukit Aman’s Death in Custody Investigation Unit and the Integrity and Standard Compliance Department to start a formal investigation.
Kuala Lumpur police said Noorizwan’s arrest prior to his death followed standard operating procedures and noted that official postmortem and chemistry reports are still pending.
Malaysian police have come under heavy public scrutiny over dozens of cases of deaths in detention over the years, sparking calls for police reform and the Independent Police Complaints and Misconduct Commission.
Civil society organisations have persistently pointed out that custodial deaths stem from systemic issues, including physical abuse during interrogation, medical neglect, poor lockup conditions, and inadequate oversight mechanisms.

Title: Last phone pings of 54 missing Malaysians traced to Nepal glacial flood site, foreign minister tells Parliament
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — The last signals emitted from the mobile phones of the missing Malaysians in Nepal were traced directly to the location hit by a “glacial tsunami”, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan told the Dewan Rakyat.
Fifty-four Malaysians are among the more than 5,500 people still unaccounted for after a major glacial collapse caused a massive flash flood that buried settlements in the country’s northern mountainous region bordering Tibet, killing between 1,300 to 1,400 people.
“Where the tsunami (flash floods) path occurred, and the last pings we received, they were all at that location,” Mohamad said during Question Time.
All 54 are believed to be dead, but Putrajaya said the Nepalese government often waits for up to 12 years to issue missing or death certificates for natural disaster cases, which has prompted families of those missing to call for government intervention.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had requested an executive order from Nepal’s Prime Minister to shorten the waiting period for issuing death certificates in disaster cases, Mohamad told Parliament.
The Nepalese government agreed to issue an executive order reducing the process to 45 days, according to the minister.
“We are currently monitoring and reviewing the contents of the order,” Mohamad said, adding that the expedited time frame will help family members resolve administrative and legal matters following the tragedy.

Title: Govt urges Malaysians to uninstall Waze over Israeli data laws, stops short of blanket ban
Article:
SEPANG, Oct 22 — The government has urged Malaysians to uninstall Waze over concerns that users’ personal and movement data could fall under Israeli jurisdiction.
National Security Council director-general for National Security Raja Datuk Nushirwan Zainal Abidin, however, said there will not be a blanket ban issued to preserve individual freedom of choice.
“The government is balancing national security considerations with human rights, freedom of expression and the freedom to choose.
“We always need to strike a balance between security and human rights consideration and freedom of expression, freedom to choose,” Nushirwan told a press conference at the National Cyber Security Agency (Nasca), National Security Council (NSC) headquarters.
Nushirwan said the concerns went beyond technology and instead concerned the legal framework governing the collection and use of personal data, pointing to Waze Mobile Ltd’s terms of use, which stipulate that the agreement is governed by Israeli law.
He said the government would not compromise on the use of Malaysians’ data and the sovereignty of national information.
To illustrate the importance of controlling data, Nushirwan compared it to fuel for a car, saying applications and artificial intelligence platforms depended on data to function.
“If we look at a car, no matter how great the model is, without fuel you cannot use the car, so this fuel is similar to data — data is actually the fuel for any application or AI platform, including Waze.
“If we supply data indiscriminately, it is as though we are relying on a source of fuel that we cannot trust,” he said.
Nushirwan said Malaysia needed to own and control its citizens’ data to protect national information sovereignty.
As of yesterday, the government has issued a ban on the usage of Waze by all civil servants when performing official duties.
“They have been encouraged to uninstall the application from their personal devices as well.
“The application could continue collecting data even when users were not actively using it, depending on its permissions and device settings.
“So the government is also encouraging the public to consider uninstalling Waze and switch to local navigation applications such as TuJu, developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority (LLM), or other available alternatives,” Nushirwan said.
When asked why the government would not ban Waze entirely, Nushirwan said a blanket prohibition would place greater emphasis on security at the expense of personal freedom.
By leaving the decision to individual users, he said, the government hoped Malaysians would make informed choices after understanding the potential implications of sharing their data with platforms governed by foreign laws.
“If they are willing for their data to go to Israel, and any legal disputes to be decided by Israeli courts, that is a matter of their own discretion,” he said.
Nushirwan described the increased public attention on cybersecurity and locally developed applications following the announcement as a positive development, adding that greater control over data was important to Malaysia’s ambition to become an AI-producing nation.
He additionally stressed that the implementation of the directive on civil servants’ usage of Waze is effective immediately.
“The directive is effective immediately. In terms of implementation, there are procedures in place.
“In general, we leave it to the respective departments’ discretion.
“In any case, a breach of any directive from the Chief Secretary to the Government (KSN) carries implications for disciplinary action,” Nushirwan said.
He was responding to reporters’ questions regarding how the government will monitor the execution of the ban on Waze for civil servants.

TuJu on the way
According to LLM deputy director general (operation) Mohammed Ridzuan Jahidin, TuJu offers an alternative for motorists seeking a locally developed navigation application.
“Its first version was launched in November 2025, offering navigation, CCTV-related functions and traffic feedback to alert users to incidents along their journeys.
“The second version adds features including information on electric vehicle-related facilities, roadblocks and saved destinations.
“It also allows users to identify where they have parked their vehicles, including in large parking areas,” he said.
He added that TuJu is in the midst of making its upgraded version 2.0 available to all mobile phone operating systems.
“The iOS version is currently undergoing final testing before its release on the App Store.
“It will likely be released by end of this year,” Mohammed Ridzuan said when met separately.
Nushirwan said the government hoped the approach would raise public awareness of cybersecurity and encourage Malaysians to consider locally developed technology.
Civil servants have been banned from using the Waze navigation app with immediate effect, following a decision by the National Cyber Security Committee (JKSN) at its meeting yesterday.
In a letter dated October 20, Chief Secretary to the Government (KSN) Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar said the JKSN Meeting No. 3 of 2026 was chaired by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
Shamsul Azri said all secretaries-general and department heads must ensure the decision is communicated to officers under their supervision, including related agencies and departments, for immediate implementation.
On Tuesday, the Prime Minister encouraged the public to use the local TuJu app, developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority (LLM), as an alternative for road navigation.
Anwar said the recommendation followed security risks to users’ information and movement data from using Waze, which is bound under Israeli government laws.
TuJu was developed by LLM in collaboration with Prosignal Consortium Sdn Bhd and launched by Works Minister Datuk Seri Alexander Nanta Linggi last November.
